title: Vintage Doctor

gui-opened-folder: Opened the folder. If you don't see it, it is behind the game's window.

questions-console: Every page is a command: /doctor crash, perf, mods, mod [mod id], log [mod id], startup, files, patches, changes, world, item [code], craft [code], bugreport [mod id], api. A fix: /doctor fix [id] [argument].

btn-move-older: Move the {0} older one(s) out of the Mods folder
btn-profile: Measure where the time goes ({0} seconds)
btn-remove-items: Remove the {0} items lying on the ground (can't be undone)
btn-repack: Repack {0} the right way (the original is kept)
btn-reset-config: Move {0} aside so a fresh one is written
btn-reset-config-default: Start {0} afresh (the old one is kept)
btn-api-docs: How to hand the doctor your own checks
cmd-noprivilege: The server's report is for players with the '{0}' privilege. Your own game's half opens with Ctrl+Shift+D or .doctor if you have Vintage Doctor installed.
cmd-fix-usage: Which fix? /doctor fix [id] [argument] - the ids are shown after each fix in the pages.
join-unclean: The game didn't close properly last time.
join-problems: The check-up found {0} problem(s) and {1} warning(s).
join-how: Press Ctrl+Shift+D or type /doctor to see what and why.
why-sameassembly: Code with the same name was loaded twice: the mod is in the Mods folder twice, it was updated while the game was running, or two different mods have a .dll with the same name. Close the game completely and start it again; if it comes back, look for the two mods.
why-missingassembly: The mod needs a code library that isn't there: a mod it depends on is missing or too old, or its download is incomplete.
why-version: The mod calls something that doesn't exist in this version of the game (or of another mod it uses): it was built for a different version. Update the mod, or use the game version it was made for.
why-harmony: One of the mod's code patches doesn't fit this version of the game. Mods that patch the game's code usually need an update after a game update.
why-format: A text has more places for values than the game gave it values. Only that text shows wrong; nothing else is affected. The mod's author (or the translation) can fix it.
why-json: A JSON file can't be read: a missing comma or bracket, usually in a config file edited by hand or a file cut short by a crash. The message says which line.
why-memory: The game ran out of memory. More mods, a longer view distance and bigger worlds all need more; closing other programs or lowering the view distance helps.
why-diskfull: The disk is full. Free some space before playing on: a save that can't be written is how worlds get damaged.
why-savecorrupt: The save file is damaged. Make a copy of it before anything else, then try the game's repair mode (in single player: the world's settings in the world list).
why-fileaccess: A file couldn't be opened because something else holds it or the game may not write there: an antivirus, a cloud-sync folder, a second copy of the game, or a read-only folder.
why-graphics: This comes from drawing, not from the world: a graphics driver that is out of date, a shader mod, or a setting the graphics card can't do.
why-network: A connection problem between this computer and the other side, not a fault in the world or a mod's content.
why-null: The code used something that wasn't there. That is a bug in the code named in the trace; nothing you set up wrong.
why-bug: A bug in the code named in the trace: it met a situation its author didn't expect.
crash-none: No crash reports: the game hasn't crashed on this side.
crash-none-why: The game writes one to Logs/{0} each time it crashes.
crash-unreadable: The crash log couldn't be read: {0}
crash-older: {0} older crash reports are further up in the file.
crash-othergame: That was on game version {0}; this is {1}.
crash-mod-gone: {0} {1} was installed then and isn't any more.
crash-mod-updated: {0} was version {1} then and is {2} now: the update may have fixed it.
crash-mod-same: {0} {1} is the same version that crashed.
crash-nomod: The game didn't name a mod and no mod's code is in the trace, so this may be the game itself, a mod that changes the game's code without showing in the trace, or the computer (memory, graphics driver).
crash-harmony: Code patches on the code that crashed belong to: {0}
crash-advice-mod: Look for an update of that mod; if it keeps crashing, switch it off and tell its author (the report below has what they need).
crash-advice-updated: The mod has been updated since. If it doesn't crash again, this is done with.
crash-advice-nomod: If it happens again, try without the mods you added or updated last, and post the report on the game's forum or Discord.
unclean-title: The game didn't close properly last time ({0}), and left no crash report
unclean-why: It was closed from outside (Task Manager, the console window's X, a shutdown), lost power, ran out of memory, or froze in the graphics driver: none of those leave a crash report.
unclean-advice: If it keeps happening while you play, watch the memory card below and update the graphics driver. A world closed this way can lose its last few minutes.
closedby-title: {0} closed the game last time ({1}), on purpose
closedby-title-why: {0} closed the game last time ({1}), on purpose: {2}
closedby-why: {0} told the doctor before it closed the game, so the game not closing the normal way then is no fault and no crash.
log-nofile: The log file {0} isn't there, so what happened at start-up can't be read.
start-clean: All {0} mod(s) loaded and started without the game reporting a problem.
start-clean-why: Read from this session's log: mods the game left out, mods that threw an error while starting, patches that didn't fit.
start-failed-why: The game carries on without the part that failed, so the mod is only half there: its blocks may exist while what they do is missing.
start-failed-advice: Look for an update of {0} that fits this game version, check it has every mod it needs, or switch it off. Its author needs the lines above.
start-skipped: {0} mod(s) were left out because something they need is missing: {1}
start-skipped-why: The game doesn't load a mod whose requirements aren't met, so nothing of these mods is in the game.
start-skipped-advice: Install what they need (the name after 'needs' is a mod id, with the lowest version that will do), or remove them.
start-blocked: {0} mod(s) were stopped by the Mod DB's block list
start-blocked-why: The Mod DB keeps a list of mod versions known to break things badly; the game refuses to load those. A newer version of the mod is usually fine.
start-duplicates: {0} mod(s) are in the Mods folder more than once
start-duplicates-why: The game loads only the newest copy. The spare copies are harmless but confusing, and a spare copy of a mod with code can stop it loading at all.
start-cyclic: Mods that may need each other in a circle: {0}
start-cyclic-why: Each waits for the other to load first, so the order they load in is a guess. If one of them misbehaves, this is why.
start-compile: A mod made of source code (.cs files) failed to compile
start-compile-why: The game compiles such mods itself as it starts; the log has the compiler's errors. The mod isn't running.
start-patches-why: A patch is how one mod changes another's (or the game's) blocks, items and recipes. One that doesn't fit is skipped, so that change isn't in the game: the thing it was for behaves as if the mod weren't there.
start-patches-advice: Usually the patching mod is made for another version of what it patches. Its author can fix the patch; an update may already have.
start-unresolved: {0} recipe(s) or drop(s) name things that don't exist, by the mod of the missing thing: {1}
start-unresolved-why: The game skips those recipes. Usually the mod expects another mod (or another version of one) to be installed.
log-clean: No errors in the log this session.
log-clean-warnings: No errors in the log this session ({0} kind(s) of warnings, {1} line(s)).
log-clean-mod: Nothing from {0} in the log this session.
log-errors: {0} kind(s) of errors in the log this session ({1} line(s)), and {2} kind(s) of warnings
log-errors-why: An error in the log doesn't always show in the game, but each is something that didn't work as its author meant. The ones that repeat, and the ones from a mod you're having trouble with, are the ones to look at.
log-errors-mod: {0}: {1} kind(s) of errors in the log this session ({2} line(s))
log-errors-nomod: {0} kind(s) of errors in the log this session that no mod could be named for ({1} line(s))
log-nomod: The game, or a mod that couldn't be told
log-spam: The same message was written {0} times: {1}
log-spam-why: Whatever causes it happens over and over, and writing it out that often slows the game by itself.
log-summary: {0} kind(s) of errors ({1} line(s)) and {2} kind(s) of warnings ({3} line(s)) in {4}, most frequent first. The same message counts once however often it was written.
log-truncated: The log is {0}, too big to read whole: the start of the session and the latest part were read, the middle left out.
log-mod-title: {0}: {1} kind(s) of errors, {2} kind(s) of warnings
folder-notscanned: Not looked at on this side.
folder-clean: {0} mod file(s) in {1} folder(s), nothing wrong with them.
folder-unreadable-why: The zip is damaged, most often a download that was cut short. The game can't load it.
folder-archive: {0} is an archive the game can't read
folder-archive-why: The game only loads .zip files (and folders).
folder-archive-advice: Unpack it and look inside: if there is a .zip, that is the mod; if there are loose files with a modinfo.json, put them in a folder of their own in Mods.
folder-partial: {0} is a download that didn't finish
folder-partial-advice: Download the mod again, and remove this leftover.
folder-innerzip-why: The mod was zipped twice (some sites and browsers do that). The game looks for modinfo.json at the top of the zip and doesn't find it.
folder-nested: {0} has its files one folder down, in '{1}', so the game can't see the mod
folder-nested-why: The game looks for modinfo.json at the top. This happens when a folder is zipped instead of what's in it.
folder-nested-advice: Move what is inside '{0}' up one level.
folder-source: {0} is a mod's source code, not the mod
folder-source-why: It has a project file and no built code: this is what the author works on (GitHub's green 'Code' button gives this). The mod to install is under Releases, or on the Mod DB.
folder-nomodinfo: {0} isn't a mod: it has no modinfo.json
folder-nomodinfo-why: The game tries to load everything in the Mods folder and reports an error for this at every start.
folder-modinfo-why: The game can't tell what this mod is, so it doesn't load it. The mod's author has to fix the file.
folder-backslash: {0} was packed with '\' in its file names, so nothing in it loads on this computer
folder-backslash-windows: {0} was packed with '\' in its file names: fine on Windows, but nothing in it loads on a Linux or Mac server
folder-backslash-why: Some Windows tools write folder separators the wrong way round into a zip. Windows reads them anyway; Linux and macOS see one long file name instead of folders, so the mod has no blocks, items or textures.
folder-duplicate-why: The game loads only the newest. The game's own 1-click install leaves the old file next to the new one.
folder-toonew: {0} mod(s) are made for a newer game than this one ({1})
folder-toonew-why: The game refuses these, or they fail when they call something this version doesn't have. Update the game, or get the mod's older release for this version.
folder-install: {0} mod(s) sit in the game's own install folder
folder-install-why: They work, but updating or reinstalling the game can wipe that folder. The Mods folder in the game's data folder is the safe place.
folder-tested: Every file in {0} zip(s) was read to the end.
folder-testing: {0} more zip(s) are still being read to the end: run the checks again in a moment.
configs-clean: {0} config file(s) read without a problem.
configs-error: The config folder couldn't be read: {0}
configs-broken: The config file {0} can't be read
configs-empty-why: A crash, a full disk or a power cut while the file was being saved leaves it empty. The mod it belongs to then starts with its defaults, or fails to start.
configs-broken-why: The file isn't valid JSON any more (a missing comma or bracket after editing by hand, most often). The mod it belongs to then starts with its defaults, or fails to start.
configs-advice: Open it in a text editor and fix the line the message names, or let the mod write a fresh one.
configs-game-why: This is one of the game's own files. The game replaces a file it can't read with a fresh one, and your settings in it are lost.
configs-game-advice: Make a copy of {0} before starting the game again if you want to rescue what's in it.
fix-unknown: There is no fix called '{0}' on this side.
fix-noserver: That fix is done by the server, and the server doesn't have Vintage Doctor.
fix-badfile: '{0}' isn't a file the doctor may touch (it only moves files in ModConfig and the Mods folders it listed).
fix-ownconfig: The doctor leaves its own config file alone.
fix-reset-config-done: Moved {0} to {1}. A fresh one is written the next time its mod starts (restart the game or the server).
fix-notzip: {0} isn't a zip the doctor can repack.
fix-repack-done: Repacked {0} ({1} file names changed); the original is in {2}. Restart the game for it to load.
fix-move-loaded: {0} is a mod the game has loaded; switch it off instead of moving it.
fix-exists: There already is a {0} in that folder.
fix-unwrap-bad: {0} isn't a mod either, so nothing was changed.
fix-unwrap-done: Took out {0}; the outer zip is in {1}. Restart the game for it to load.
fix-disable-refused: {0} isn't something the doctor switches off.
fix-disable-done-client: {0} is switched off from the next time the game starts. It comes back on in the main menu's Mod Manager.
fix-disable-done-server: {0} is switched off from the next server start (the world's list of disabled mods in serverconfig.json; take it out there to bring it back).
fix-disable-singleplayer: In single player, mods are switched off on your own computer: use the button for {0} under 'Your game', or the Mod Manager in the main menu.
fix-disable-manual: The doctor couldn't reach the server's list. By hand: stop the server and add "{0}" to WorldConfig.DisabledMods in serverconfig.json.
fix-profile-started: Measuring for {0} seconds. The page opens by itself when it's done.
fix-setting-bad: '{0}' isn't a setting the doctor changes.
fix-setting-done: Set {0} to {1}. It can be changed back in the game's graphics settings.
fix-command-off: Fixes that run a command are switched off on this server (AllowCommandFixes in ModConfig/vintagedoctor.json).
fix-command-server: The command {0} has to be run on the server.
fix-command-done: Ran {0} as the server console; its answer is in the server's console.
perf-tick-early: The server has only just started; give it a minute before judging its speed.
perf-tick-ok: The server keeps up: a tick every {0} ms ({1} a second).
perf-tick-slow: The server is falling behind: a tick every {0} ms ({1} a second), {2} long pauses in the last 10 minutes (the worst {3} ms)
perf-tick-slow-why: The world moves in steps ('ticks'), {0} ms apart when all is well. When a step takes longer, everything stutters at once: animals jump, doors open late, blocks you break come back for a moment.
perf-tick-slow-advice: Press the measuring button: after 20 seconds this page shows what the time went on, by part of the game and by mod.
perf-tick-detail: Last minute: average {0} ms, 95% under {1} ms, worst {2} ms ({3} ticks).
perf-overloads: The game itself logged {0} tick(s) over half a second this session (the worst {1} ms; {2} in the last 10 minutes).
perf-entities-ok: {0} creatures and things loaded ({1} items on the ground), {2} chunks, {3} player(s).
perf-entities-many: {0} creatures and things are loaded ({1} of them items on the ground)
perf-items-many: {0} items are lying on the ground
perf-entities-why: Every one of them is moved and checked each tick. Thousands (a farm that grew out of hand, a machine spilling items) slow the whole server.
perf-entities-error: The loaded creatures couldn't be counted: {0}
perf-memory-ok: Memory: the game holds {0} of the {1} it can use.
perf-memory-high: Memory is nearly full: the game holds {0} of {1} ({2}%)
perf-memory-why: When memory runs out the game stutters while it frees some, and in the end crashes without a useful report.
perf-memory-advice-client: Lower the view distance, close other programs, and restart the game after long sessions.
perf-memory-advice-server: Lower the server's view distance (MaxChunkRadius), restart it once a day, or give it more memory.
perf-memory-detail: {0} in the game's own objects; {1} full clean-ups so far; {2} processor threads.
perf-profile-running: Measuring where the time goes... {0} seconds left.
perf-profile-what: The game can time every part of a tick: creatures, each kind of machine and block that does something, each mod's own work. The doctor switches that on for 20 seconds, adds it up, and switches it off again.
perf-profile-title: Measured for {0} seconds ({1} ticks): {2} ms of work per tick, at {3}
perf-profile-explain: The parts that took the most time, per tick. The name in square brackets is the mod the code belongs to; (N×) is how many of them ran each tick.
perf-profile-explain-client: The parts that took the most time, per frame. The name in square brackets is the mod the code belongs to; (N×) is how many of them ran each frame.
perf-profile-mods-why: Only the work the game can tell apart by its code (things that tick, windows, timers) is counted against a mod; what a mod adds to creatures or to the world's generation isn't. A mod with many machines running is not broken for being first here.
prof-mtasks: Work handed to the main thread
gfx-software: The game is drawing without a graphics card: {0}
gfx-software-why: No graphics driver is in use, so the processor does the drawing. That is many times slower and is why the game crawls.
gfx-software-advice: Install the graphics card's driver from its maker (Nvidia, AMD or Intel), not the one Windows picks.
gfx-fps-early: The frame rate is measured over the last minute; ask again in a moment.
gfx-fps-stutter: {0} frames a second, but it drops to {1} in its slowest moments
gfx-fps-why: Under about 30 the game feels heavy. The buttons below turn down the settings that cost the most; the measuring button shows which part of drawing takes the time.
gfx-stutter-why: Smooth most of the time with short freezes: usually new land being loaded (view distance), memory being freed, or the server pausing.
gfx-fps-detail: Last minute: average {0} ms a frame, 95% under {1} ms, worst {2} ms.
gfx-suggest-advice: Change one, play for a moment, and press Run checks again to see what it did.
gfx-gldebug: The graphics debug mode is on
gfx-gldebug-why: It checks every drawing call and slows drawing a lot. It is only for hunting graphics bugs.
gfx-occlusion: Occlusion culling is off: the game draws caves and rooms you can't see.
hotkeys-ok: No two controls share a key.
hotkeys-clash: {0} pair(s) of controls share a key
hotkeys-why: Only one of the two gets the key press, so the other seems dead.
hotkeys-advice: Give one of them another key: Esc, then Settings, then Controls (mods' keys are in the list too).
versus-ok: Every mod you share with the server ({0}) is the same version on both.
versus-different: {0} mod(s) are a different version on your computer than on the server
versus-why: The two halves of a mod talk to each other; different versions can misread each other. Things then look right on one side and wrong on the other.
versus-onlymine: {0} mod(s) run only on your computer
versus-onlymine-why: That is fine for mods that only change what you see. The server knows nothing of them.
mods-help: {0} mod(s) loaded; {1} have something against them. A mod's page shows everything the doctor knows about it.
mods-errors: {0} kind(s) of errors in the log
mods-skipped: {0} more left out by the game: {1}
mod-identity-detail: Mod id {0}; {1} mod; runs on: {2}; file {3}
mod-core: This is part of the game itself.
mod-unknown: No mod called '{0}' is loaded, and none is in the Mods folder.
mod-skipped: {0} is installed but was left out: it needs {1}
mod-notloaded-file: {0} is in the Mods folder ({1}) but the game didn't load it
mod-notloaded-file-why: It may be switched off in the Mod Manager, be made for the other side only (a client mod on a server), or be an older copy of a mod installed twice.
mod-dep-game: The game: wants {0} or newer, this is {1}
mod-patches-failed: {0} of its JSON patches didn't apply
mod-unresolved: {0} recipe(s) or drop(s) name things of this mod that don't exist
mod-crashes: Named in {0} crash report(s); the last on {1} ({2})
mod-content: In the game from this mod: {0} blocks, {1} items, {2} creatures.
mod-content-none: Nothing with this mod's id is in the game
mod-content-none-why: For a mod that adds things, that means its files didn't load (see the Mods folder page). A mod that only changes other things has nothing of its own, and this is fine.
mod-configs-why: If the mod acts oddly after an update, an old config is a common reason: starting it afresh puts every setting back to the mod's defaults (the old file is kept in the doctor's backups).
mod-harmony: It changes the game's code in {0} place(s), {1} of them shared with other mods
mod-profile: In the last measured run its code took {0} ms of the {1} ms of work per tick.
modcheck-failed: {0}'s own check '{1}' stopped with an error: {2}
modcheck-failed-why: That is a bug in the mod's check, not in your game; the mod's author will want to know.
recommend-title: {0} works better with {1}, which isn't installed
changes-first: This is the first session the doctor has seen here, so there is nothing to compare with yet.
changes-first-why: From now on it notes the mods and their versions at every start, and shows here what changed.
changes-none: The same mods and versions as last time ({0}).
changes-title: Since last time ({0}): {1} mod(s) added, {2} updated, {3} removed.
changes-why: When something worked before and doesn't now, what changed in between is the first suspect.
changes-removed-why: Blocks and items of a removed mod stay in the world as unknown ('?') things until the mod is back.
patches-none: No mod changes the game's code.
patches-error: The code patches couldn't be read: {0}
patches-title: {0} mod(s) change the game's code in {1} place(s)
patches-why: Mods patch the game's own code where it offers no other way in. It is normal, but it is also what breaks first when the game updates, and two mods patching the same place can get in each other's way.
patches-shared: {0} change the same {1} place(s) in the game's code
patches-shared-why: Each line is one piece of the game's code and what each mod does to it. Mods that only run something before or after the game's code usually get along. It goes wrong when one of them stops the game's code from running, which the other counted on, or when both rewrite it. If something these mods have to do with misbehaves, these are the places to tell their authors about.
patches-shared-none: No two mods change the same place in the game's code.
patches-shared-more: {0} more group(s) of mods change the same places in the game's code
sec-tags: Texts with formatting tags out of place
tags-mod: {0}'s texts have formatting tags out of place: {1} error(s) about them in the log this session
tags-mod-maybe: {0}'s texts are the likely cause of {1} error(s) about formatting tags in the log this session
tags-nomod: {0} error(s) about formatting tags in the log this session that no mod could be named for
tags-lang: {0}: {1} of its texts have formatting tags out of place
tags-ok: No formatting tags out of place: no errors about them in the log, and none in the mods' texts.
tags-likely: (likely: the same mistake, at another place)
tags-what-stray: a > with no < before it, at character {0}
tags-what-never: </{0}> with no <{0}> before it, at character {1}
tags-what-first: </{0}> while <{1}> is still open, at character {2}
tags-what-open: <{0}> is opened and never closed, so it clashes with the formatting the game puts around the text
tags-why: The game reads < and > in texts (chat, item descriptions, tooltips, the handbook) as formatting tags. A > on its own, or a closing tag that doesn't match, makes it write an error every time the text is shown; the text is usually still shown. The error never says whose text it was, so the doctor reads every mod's texts the way the game does and finds the ones that make that very error. The whole text is also in {0}, on the line after each error.
tags-lang-why: Nothing in this session's errors was traced to these texts, but each would make the game write an error when it shows it: the game reads < and > in texts as formatting tags.
tags-advice: Tell {0}'s author which texts these are (the names above are their keys in the mod's lang file): a > that isn't part of a tag has to be written >, and a < as <.
tags-advice-nomod: The whole text of each is in {0}, on the line after the error: it usually shows whose it is.
patch-ends: steps in when it ends or fails
patches-rewritten-why: Each line is one piece of the game's code and what each mod does to it. Where two mods rewrite the same piece, each expects to find it as the game shipped it: the second may not find what it looks for, so one of them can stop working, or the game can crash there.
jsonpatches-none: {0} JSON patches in {1} files, no two mods replacing the same thing.
jsonpatches-clash: {0} thing(s) are replaced or removed by more than one mod
jsonpatches-why: When two mods set the same value, the one loaded last wins and the other's change is gone, without any error. If a mod's change seems to do nothing, look for it here.
world-disk-ok: {0} free where the world is saved.
world-disk-low: Only {0} free where the world is saved
world-disk-critical: The disk the world is saved on is almost full: {0} left
world-disk-why: A save that can't be written is how worlds get damaged. Backups and logs fill a disk quietly.
world-disk-advice: Free some space now (old backups in the Backups folder, old logs) before playing on.
world-missing: This world has {0} blocks and {1} items from mods that aren't here any more: {2}
world-missing-changed: {0}: {1} (such as {2}); the mod is installed but no longer has them
world-missing-none: Nothing in this world comes from a mod that isn't installed.
world-missing-why: The game keeps them as unknown ('?') blocks and items so nothing is lost. They do nothing until their mod is back.
world-missing-advice: Put the mod back (the same or a newer version) and they come back as they were. Without it they are harmless and can be broken or thrown away.
world-time: Time in this world runs {0} times as fast as normal
world-time-why: A setting or a mod changed it. Everything on a timer (crops, storms, food going off) comes round that much sooner or later in real time.
world-time-ok: Time runs at the normal pace.
item-holdit: Hold the item in question, then ask again (or type /doctor item [code]).
item-notfound: There is no block or item '{0}' in this game.
item-help: A code looks like game:ingot-copper; the handbook and the creative inventory show it when extended debug info is on.
item-kind: {0} with the code {1}; class {2}; run by {3}
item-entityclass: Keeps its own data and does things over time as: {0}
item-missing: {0} is a placeholder: the real block or item isn't in the game
item-missing-why-gone: It came from the mod '{0}', which isn't installed.
item-missing-why-changed: It came from {0}, which is installed but no longer has it (it changed between versions).
item-notinlog: The log has no error or warning that mentions it.
block-lookat: Look at the block in question, then ask again.
block-entity: It is run by the code {0}, from {1}.
block-noentity: This block should have data of its own ('{0}') and has none
block-noentity-why: The block is there but the part that makes it do things is not: it will sit dead. Breaking it and placing it again usually brings it back. It happens when a mod was missing for a while or failed to start.
craft-holdit: Hold one of what you want to craft (from the creative inventory, say), or type /doctor craft [code].
craft-help: The doctor then lists every crafting-grid recipe that makes it and what stands in the way.
craft-none-why: It may be made another way (smithing, knapping, clay forming, a barrel, cooking, a mod's own machine), be found or traded, or its recipe may have failed to load. The handbook (H while pointing at it) shows every way the game knows.
craft-unresolved: {0} recipe(s) of {1} were skipped by the game at start-up
craft-trait: Recipe {0} is only for characters with the trait '{1}': {2}
craft-trait-missing: Recipe {0} needs the trait '{1}', which your character doesn't have: {2}
craft-trait-why: Some recipes belong to a character class (a tailor's clothes, a blackguard's armour). Other classes can't craft them at all; the grid simply stays empty.
craft-disabled-why: A mod or the server's settings turned this recipe off.
craft-tips: If the grid stays empty with a recipe that should work: check the exact variant of each ingredient (the wood or metal type), that tools are in the grid, and that no ingredient is a stack of a different kind than it looks.
api-help: Other mods can hand the doctor their own checks, fixes, pages and explanations for log messages. This page shows what has been handed over on this side.
api-counts: {0} check(s), {1} fix(es) and {2} page(s) from other mods; {3} log message(s) the doctor can explain.
api-docs: Three ways in: a few lines of C#, the event bus (no reference to the doctor needed), or a JSON file in your mod's assets (no code at all).
bugreport-help: Everything a mod's author or the game's forum needs, with addresses, player ids and user folders taken out. Read it over, then post it with what you were doing and what you expected.
bugreport-send: Copy this page (the button below) or attach the saved file.
start-files-failed: {0} file(s) in the Mods folder aren't mods the game can load: {1}
start-files-failed-why: The game tries everything in the Mods folder at every start, and reports an error for each of these. The Mods folder page says what each one is and offers the fix.
reason-innerzip: it holds another zip ({0}) instead of the mod
reason-nested: the mod sits one folder down inside it (in '{0}')
reason-nomodinfo: it has no modinfo.json, so it isn't a mod
reason-source: it is a mod's source code, not the mod
sec-clashes: Mods getting in each other's way, or their own
q-clashes: Are any mods getting in each other's way?
and-has-errors: This mod has errors in this session.
missing-title: {0}: {1} block(s) or item(s) need code that isn't in the game ({2})
missing-why: Each of these names a piece of code that should make it work, and no loaded mod has that code: the mod's own code didn't load, it needs another mod that isn't installed, or this version of the mod doesn't match its files. They are in the game but act like plain blocks and items: machines don't open, tools don't do their job.
missing-why-startfailed: {0}'s code didn't start (the start-up page has the error), so the things it adds are in the game but do nothing: machines don't open, tools don't do their job.
missing-advice: Update the mod and install every mod its page lists as required. For a mod of your own: the name in the file has to be exactly the one given to RegisterBlockClass, RegisterItemClass or RegisterBlockEntityClass.
missing-none: Every block and item that needs code has it.
types-broken: {0}: {1} of its files couldn't be read, so what they describe isn't in the game
types-broken-why: Each of these files has a mistake in it (most often a missing comma or bracket) or uses something this version of the game doesn't know, and the game skipped the whole file: the blocks, items or recipes in it don't exist. The mod's page has the game's own error for each, with the place.
targets-missing: {0} tries to change {1} file(s) that aren't there
targets-missing-why: A patch changes one thing inside another file. These files don't exist in this version of the game (or of the mod they belong to): they were renamed, moved or removed in an update, and the mod hasn't caught up. Whatever those patches were for doesn't happen.
targets-optional: {0} has {1} patch(es) for mods that aren't installed ({2})
targets-optional-why: That is how one mod supports another, and harmless: the game writes each one into the log as an error, but nothing is missing.
targets-none: No mod tries to change a file that isn't there.
ignoredcode-title: {0} has code in it ({2}) but calls itself a {1} mod, so the game leaves the code out
ignoredcode-why: The game only runs code from mods whose modinfo.json says "type": "code". Whatever this mod's code was meant to do doesn't happen; its blocks, items and recipes still load.
ignoredcode-advice: Tell the mod's author. Changing the type to "code" in the modinfo.json inside the zip puts it right.
notloaded-title: {0} has {1} block and item file(s), but none of its blocks or items are in the game
notloaded-why: The mod loaded, but nothing it describes arrived: its files are in the wrong folders inside the zip, every one of them failed to load (the start-up page has the errors), or they are switched off in the mod's settings.
notloaded-none: Every mod that has block and item files has them in the game.
bundled-title: {0} brings its own copy of {1}, which the game already has.
bundled-why: Only one copy of a code library can be in use, and the game's own comes first. A mod's copy is at best ignored; when it is a different version, the mod fails with "method not found" or "could not load file or assembly".
bundled-advice: Nothing needs doing while the mod works. If it has errors, an update from its author is the fix: the mod has to be built for the library the game comes with.
bundled-none: No mod brings its own copy of a library the game or another mod already has.
btn-strip: Take the game's libraries out of {0} (the original is kept)
shared-dll-title: {0} is in more than one mod: {1}.
shared-dll-why: The game loads a code library by name once. Whichever mod loads first decides the version; the other gets that copy too, and fails if it needed a different one.
replaced-clash: {0} file(s) are replaced by more than one mod: only one copy of each is used
replaced-clash-why: When two mods ship the same file, the game takes one and drops the other without a word. One of these mods isn't doing all it was meant to. Which one wins depends on the order the game loads them in.
replaced-clash-advice: Check both mods' pages for a note about each other. If they do the same job, keep one. Mods that change a file with a patch instead of replacing it can work side by side.
replaced-look: {0} texture, shape or sound file(s) are replaced by more than one mod
replaced-look-why: Only looks and sounds: one mod's version shows and the other's doesn't. Common with texture packs, and harmless.
replaced-game: {0} replaces {1} of the game's own files outright
replaced-game-why: A mod can change a file of the game with a patch (one value) or by shipping its own copy of the whole file. A whole copy also throws away whatever the game's updates and other mods' patches changed in that file, so it is the first thing to look at when something else stops working.
replaced-game-old: {0} mod(s) made for an older game replace {1} of the game's own files (the game is {2})
replaced-game-old-why: These mods ship whole copies of the game's files as they were in an older version. Everything the game has changed in those files since is undone: recipes and items that went missing, things from the update that don't work, shaders that give a black screen or stop the game from starting.
replaced-game-old-advice: Look for an update of each. If something from the last game update is missing or broken, try without these mods first.
replaced-none: No two mods replace the same file, and none replaces the game's own.
oldmods-broken: {0} mod(s) with code were made for an older game than {1} and have errors now: {2}
oldmods-why: Mods that add code are built against one version of the game. After a game update most keep working, but when one of them has errors, the version is the first suspect.
oldmods-advice: Update these first. If there is no update, the mod's page or comments usually say whether it works on this version.
oldmods-fine: {0} mod(s) with code were made for an older game than {1} and show no errors
oldmods-fine-why: Nothing to do: mods often keep working across game updates. If something odd turns up later, these are the ones to check first.
shadow-title: {0} recipe(s) have exactly the same ingredients as another recipe that makes something else
shadow-title-item: Another recipe has exactly the same ingredients and makes something else
shadow-why: The crafting grid can only offer one result for one set of ingredients, so only one of each pair can ever be crafted. This happens when two mods each add a recipe without knowing of the other.
shadow-advice: Many mods can switch single recipes off in their config. Otherwise tell both authors: one of them has to change an ingredient.
shadow-none: No recipe from a mod has the same ingredients as another recipe that makes something else ({0} crafting recipes looked at).
names-missing: {0}: {1} of its {2} things show a code instead of a name ("{3}")
names-why: The mod's texts didn't load, or it has none in this language: its lang file has a mistake, is in the wrong folder, or the mod was packed without it. Everything still works; only the names are missing.
names-none: Every mod's blocks and items have names.
mod-foreign: It replaces {0} of the game's own files and puts {1} file(s) into other mods' folders
folder-misplaced: {0} has code where the game doesn't accept it ({1}), so the game won't load it
folder-misplaced-why: The game's rule: a mod's .dll files sit at the top of the zip (only libraries that aren't .NET go in a folder, native/), and .cs files sit in src/. One file elsewhere and the game refuses the whole mod.
folder-misplaced-advice: This is how the mod was packed: get it again from its page, and tell the author if the download is the same.
reason-misplaced: it has code in the wrong place ({0})
fix-strip-done: {0} was written again without {1}. The original is in {2}. It takes effect the next time the game starts.
fix-strip-none: {0} doesn't bring any library the game already has.
fix-strip-all: {0} has no code of its own besides the game's libraries, so it was left alone.
perf-memory-growing: Memory use has grown by {0} in the last {1} minutes (from {2} to {3}) and is still climbing
perf-memory-growing-why: Using a lot of memory is normal; using more every minute is not. Something keeps things it should let go of, and when the memory runs out the game freezes or crashes. Exploring new land makes memory grow for a while too, then it levels off.
why-native: The mod needs a library that isn't part of .NET, and it isn't there or isn't made for this system: a Windows-only mod on Linux or macOS, or a download that is missing files.
why-badimage: A code file is damaged or isn't made for this system. Download the mod again; if that doesn't help, the mod wasn't built for this kind of computer.
why-duplicate: Something was added under a name that is already taken: two mods add a thing with the same name, the same mod was loaded twice, or one mod adds the same thing twice. One of the two is left out, and what depends on it may misbehave.
why-packaging: The mod's zip is put together in a way the game doesn't accept: a code mod needs exactly one .dll of its own at the top of the zip. That is for the mod's author to fix; getting the mod again from its page sometimes helps.
notadded-title: {0}: {1} block(s) or item(s) couldn't be added to the game
notadded-why: The game refused them while loading. Most often something with the same name was already there: two mods, or two files of one mod, add a thing with the same name, and only the first one exists. The log has the game's reason for each.
sec-about-mods: What your mods say about it
guest-timeout: {0} said it needed a moment and then didn't answer. Its part is missing here; the log may say why.
guest-working: {0} is still putting its part together. Open the page again in a moment.
guest-fix-working: The mod behind '{0}' is working on it; the log will say when it is done.
cmd-working: A mod is still working on that. The result follows in a moment.
gui-working: A mod is still working on it...
